title: How Am I Supposed to Do That?
author: Chris Voss with Tahl Raz
wiifm: Every day you negotiate: with lenders, with landlords, with a frightened client who owes more than they can pay, with a supplier who wants a bigger cut. Today you follow Chris Voss, a policeman who became the FBI's lead international kidnapping negotiator and then took on Harvard's professors in their own classroom. His book is a toolkit for the hardest conversations: how to make people feel heard, how to get them to say no safely, and how to bargain on price. You will also learn where his claims are shaky, so you can use the tools without swallowing the myths.

ch.h: A man on the phone in Brooklyn
b: In the autumn of 1993 an armed robbery at a Chase Manhattan bank branch in Brooklyn went wrong and turned into a siege. On the telephone, trying to talk the robber out, was a comparatively new FBI negotiator named Chris Voss.

The man on the other end lied about almost everything, including how many people were inside with him. The standoff dragged on for hours. In the end nobody was killed. And Voss walked away with a correction to everything he thought he knew. He had been taught that negotiation was a contest of offers. What he had actually spent the day doing was trying to work out what the man on the line believed was happening. The offers came later, almost as an afterthought.

A caution before going further. The details Voss gives of that bank job, like many of the stories in this book, are his own recollection decades later, and they do not match the public record perfectly. That does not make them false. It makes them testimony rather than evidence, and you should read the whole book the way you would listen to a very good witness.
ch.cap: Outside the Brooklyn bank, Voss talks a robber down

ch.h: A bad knee and a crisis line
b: Voss grew up in Iowa and, by his own account, started out as a beat cop in Kansas City, Missouri, before joining the FBI in 1983. In New York he worked on the Joint Terrorism Task Force and wanted to be on a SWAT team.

A knee injury ended that hope, and what he did next shaped his life. He volunteered on a suicide crisis hotline, answering calls from people at the end of their tether. There he learned the first lesson of his trade: you cannot argue a desperate person out of despair. You can only show them that you understand where they are, and let them talk their own way back.

That experience got him into hostage negotiation. He trained at the FBI Academy at Quantico, and from 2003 to 2007 he was the Bureau's lead international kidnapping negotiator. Note the dates. The book's marketing sometimes blurs his twenty-four years in the FBI with his time as lead negotiator, which was four. He retired in 2007 and founded a consultancy, the Black Swan Group, on one bold premise: what works on a man with a gun works, with the volume turned down, on a supplier, a landlord or a hiring manager.
ch.cap: Knee wrecked, Voss answers a suicide crisis line

b: The book opens with its founding scene. Voss, an ex-cop surrounded by lawyers and business-school graduates, enrols on an executive negotiation course at Harvard Law School. In a role-play exercise he is put opposite Robert Mnookin, the head of Harvard's Program on Negotiation, and later Gabriella Blum, a professor who had negotiated for Israel. These are the people who wrote the field.
Voss wins. He does it by saying very little. Whatever they propose, he answers slowly, calmly, in a low voice: how am I supposed to do that?

Look at what that sentence does. It is a refusal with no no in it, so there is nothing to push against. It hands the other side the power, which flatters them, and at the same time it hands them your problem. Because it is an open question, courtesy obliges them to answer, which means they now have to do the work of finding a solution. Voss calls this a calibrated question: one that begins with how or what and invites the other person to solve your problem for you. It is the single most portable tool in the book. You could use it on a builder this afternoon.

Voss admits he arrived feeling out of place. He had no law degree and no business training, only years on phones with people who had guns. What surprised him was that the academics, for all their brilliance, were treating negotiation as a puzzle of offers and counter-offers to be solved logically. He was treating it as a conversation with a frightened human being. In the role-play, the human approach won.
ch.cap: At Harvard, Voss asks: how am I supposed to?

b: In the mid-2000s Haiti suffered a wave of kidnappings, and Voss's team was called in. In one case the kidnappers demanded a hundred and fifty thousand dollars for a hostage, a relative of someone the team knew.

The breakthrough came when the negotiators realised what the kidnappers actually wanted. These were not professionals running a business. They were young men who wanted money to party at the weekend. As Voss put it, they were always ready to party on Saturday night. The demand and the motive were two completely different things. Once the team understood the motive, they used it, and the deal settled at a few thousand dollars.

As with much of the book, this is Voss's own telling and the numbers cannot be checked. But the lesson survives even if the details do not. Whenever someone gives you a number, ask what the number is for. It is almost never what they said it was for. Voss calls these hidden facts black swans: unknown pieces of information that change the whole negotiation once they surface. You do not find them by being clever. You find them by making the other person comfortable enough to let one slip.

The method behind that discovery was patient, unglamorous listening. The team kept the kidnappers talking, asked open questions, noted every detail of what they said and how they said it, and gradually built a picture of who these people were and what their week looked like. The number on the table only made sense once the people behind it did.
ch.cap: The ransom is for Saturday night in Port-au-Prince

b: Voss's name for his whole discipline is tactical empathy, and he strips it of any warmth. It is not sympathy, it is not agreement, and it is not liking the person. It is understanding their situation from the inside, their fears, their limits, what they will have to explain to their own boss, and then saying it out loud so they know you have understood. The reason is practical. People who feel unheard keep repeating themselves. People who feel heard start explaining, and explanation is where the useful information lives.

The first tool is the mirror. You repeat the last one to three words the person said, or the most important one to three words, with a slight questioning lift. Then you stay silent for at least four seconds. The silence is the whole trick. People fill it, almost every time, and they fill it with more detail.

The second tool is the label. You name the emotion you can detect, starting with it seems like, it sounds like, or it looks like. Not I'm hearing that, because the word I makes the sentence about you. Then you stop talking. Naming a negative feeling takes the heat out of it. This is the part of the book with the best scientific support: psychologists have found that putting a feeling into words measurably reduces its intensity. Voss did not learn it from a laboratory. He learned it on the phone, in the dark, with armed men.

A close cousin is the accusation audit. Before a hard conversation, list every bad thing the other side might think about you, and say it first, in harsher words than they would dare. An accusation you have already made against yourself cannot be used as ammunition.

Here is how it sounds in practice. Before telling a client about a price rise or a delay, you might open with: you are probably going to think we have taken you for granted, and you are probably wondering why you should believe a word of this new schedule given the last one. Having said it, you have taken the sting out of it, and you have shown that you understand how things look from their chair, which is the one credential that matters at that moment.
ch.cap: A label, then four seconds of silence on the line

ch.h: The power of no, and that's right
b: The heart of the book is a reversal. Everyone is taught to chase yes. Voss argues that yes is often fake, a way of escaping the conversation, while no gives people what they most need before they will talk honestly: a sense of safety and control.

So he flips the usual questions. Instead of asking whether someone has a few minutes, ask whether now is a bad time to talk. Saying no is easy and costs them nothing, and having asserted control, they usually carry on talking. For a client who has gone silent, he suggests a one-line email: have you given up on this project? Almost nobody can leave it unanswered, because answering takes one word and silence concedes something.

Then the distinction worth remembering above all others. The breakthrough moment in a negotiation is not when the other person says you're right. That is a brush-off, something people say to make you stop talking. The breakthrough is when they say that's right. It means you have summarised their world so accurately that they recognise themselves in it, and they stop defending. You earn it by labelling their feelings and paraphrasing their position, and then waiting.
ch.cap: Not 'you're right' but 'that's right': the breakthrough

b: In January 2006 Jill Carroll, an American freelance reporter writing for the Christian Science Monitor, was kidnapped in Baghdad. Her interpreter, Allan Enwiya, was shot dead during the abduction. Her captors then issued deadlines on television: meet their demands or she would die by a certain date.
The date passed. Nothing happened. Another deadline came, and passed too. After eighty-two days in captivity, Carroll was released alive.

Voss was involved in the case as the FBI's lead international kidnapping negotiator, and the lesson he drew from it is one you can use in any commercial deal. Most deadlines are made up. They often cause more anxiety to the person who set them than to the person they are aimed at, because the person who announces a deadline must then decide what to do when it arrives. When you are being rushed, remember that the clock is usually someone's invention.
ch.cap: Televised deadlines come and go; 82 days pass

b: Voss does have a bargaining system, borrowed from kidnap-and-ransom work and named after Mike Ackerman, a former CIA officer who advised on kidnap response. Decide your real target. Open at sixty-five per cent of it. Then move to eighty-five, then ninety-five, then one hundred, and never move until you have used empathy and a calibrated question to make them respond first. The shrinking steps tell the other side you are close to your limit. Make the final figure precise, like thirty-seven thousand eight hundred and ninety-three pounds rather than thirty-eight thousand, because an odd number sounds calculated rather than chosen. And at the end, throw in something non-monetary they probably do not want, to show you have truly run out of money.

Voice is a tool too. Voss describes three: a warm, easygoing default; a direct, assertive voice to be used almost never; and his famous late-night radio DJ voice, slow and calm, with the tone going down at the end of a sentence. A falling tone states. A rising tone asks permission.

Two other ideas in this part rest on solid research. Quoting a range rather than a single number tends to pull people into the range, because anchoring is one of the best-established effects in behavioural economics. And people will work harder to avoid a loss than to gain the same amount, so framing the cost of not acting is powerful. Use it honestly. If the loss is not real, you are just lying with better grammar.

Voss is careful to say that the numbers are the last step, not the first. If you start haggling before you understand the other side's world, you are just trading figures in the dark. The empathy, the mirrors, the labels and the calibrated questions are what tell you where the real limits are, and only then do the percentages do their work.

The book itself was written with the journalist Tahl Raz and published in 2016, nine years after Voss left the Bureau. It became a bestseller and turned its author into one of the most quoted negotiation teachers in the world. Its success is partly a lesson in its own methods: it tells vivid stories with a gap in each, it names its enemy clearly, and it hands the reader a few short phrases they can try the same afternoon.

Voss repeats the claim that only seven per cent of a message is the words, thirty-eight per cent is tone of voice and fifty-five per cent is body language. This is a misuse of real research. The numbers come from two small 1967 studies by the psychologist Albert Mehrabian, one testing single spoken words against tone and one testing photographs of faces against tone. They involved no conversation and only measured how people judged liking when words and tone contradicted each other. Mehrabian himself has said for decades that the figures do not apply to communication in general. Delivery matters, obviously. The percentages are a myth.

His other weakness is his favourite target, Getting to Yes, the 1981 Harvard classic by Roger Fisher and William Ury, which teaches you to focus on interests, separate people from problems and know your best alternative to a deal. Voss attacks it for treating people as rational. Some of that lands, but he is attacking an old caricature: later work from the same Harvard school dealt directly with emotion. And hostage talks are one-off, high-pressure and lopsided, while most business deals are repeated, with people you will see again, where preparation and shared value matter a great deal.

So read Voss as a specialist in the hardest case. When the other side is emotional, acting in bad faith or holding all the cards, his toolkit is better than the textbook one. When you are making an ordinary deal with a reasonable person, do your preparation as well. The man who learned on a crisis line that people need to be heard before they can be moved left behind tools that work. They work best in the hands of someone who knows where they came from.
ch.cap: A great witness, but his 7-38-55 myth is struck

take: How am I supposed to do that is a refusal with nothing to push against. Use it when a lender, supplier or client asks for terms you cannot meet, and let them solve the problem.
Repeat the last few key words with a questioning lift, then stay quiet for four seconds. On sales and client calls, the detail you need usually arrives in that silence.
Start with it sounds like or it seems like, name what the other person feels, then stop. With a stressed debt client this lowers the temperature faster than any reassurance.
Before a difficult call, say the worst things they could think about you before they can. It turns ammunition into common ground.
Ask is now a bad time, or have you given up on this, instead of chasing a yes. A safe no keeps people talking; a forced yes means nothing.
Chase that's right, not you're right
Summarise their position until they say that's right. If they say you're right, they are only trying to end the conversation.
Ask what the number is for
A demand is not the same as a motive. Find out what someone actually needs the money or deadline for, and you often find a cheaper way to meet it.
Delivery matters, but the famous percentages come from narrow 1967 studies their author says do not generalise. Do not repeat them in training or pitches.

note: Voss's FBI career, his role as lead international kidnapping negotiator from 2003 to 2007, the Jill Carroll kidnapping of 2006 and her release after eighty-two days are documented. The Harvard exercise, the Haiti figures and the details of the 1993 bank siege rest on his own accounts and cannot be independently checked; contemporaneous reports place the siege in late September 1993. The 7-38-55 rule misreads Mehrabian's 1967 studies, and the experimental negotiation literature is kinder to Fisher and Ury's Getting to Yes than Voss is.

Voss's calibrated questions, which begin with how or what, are tuned to make the other side solve your problem without feeling pushed.

stories: How am I supposed to do that?

Chris Voss, an ex-cop turned FBI hostage negotiator, enrolled on an executive negotiation course at Harvard Law School, surrounded by lawyers and business graduates. In a role-play he was put opposite Robert Mnookin, head of Harvard's Program on Negotiation, one of the people who had written the field. By his own account, Voss barely said anything. Whatever they proposed, he answered slowly, in a low, calm voice: how am I supposed to do that? And he won. The sentence is a no without the word no. It flatters the other side by handing them control, and it hands them your problem to solve.
Ready to party on Saturday night

In the mid two-thousands Haiti was gripped by a wave of kidnappings, and Voss's FBI team was called in. In one case the kidnappers demanded a hundred and fifty thousand dollars. The breakthrough came from patient listening, not clever offers. The team realised these were not hardened professionals but young men who wanted money to party at the weekend. As Voss put it, they were always ready to party on Saturday night. Once the team understood what the money was for, the deal settled at a few thousand dollars. It is Voss's own telling and the figures cannot be checked, but the lesson holds: always ask what the number is for.
The deadlines that came and went

In January 2006 the American freelance reporter Jill Carroll was kidnapped in Baghdad while working for the Christian Science Monitor. Her interpreter, Allan Enwiya, was shot dead during the abduction. Her captors went on television with a deadline: meet our demands or she dies. The date passed and nothing happened. Another deadline came, and passed too. After eighty-two days she was released alive. Voss, then the FBI's lead international kidnapping negotiator, was involved in the case and drew a lesson for every business deal. Most deadlines are invented, and they often trouble the person who set them more than the person they target.
biz: Voss argues that people relax and talk when they are allowed to say no. Most follow-ups to HomeownersLoan leads who have gone quiet push for a yes, which feels like pressure and gets ignored. This week, test a WhatsApp follow-up that offers a clean exit, for example: is now a bad time to pick this back up, or would you rather we closed your enquiry? Honour every no at once and close the file. Measure reply rate, opt-outs and how many replies become completed applications, against your current message. Never pair it with a fake deadline or a hint that an offer will vanish.
Label the feeling, then be quiet

Debt Support Direct clients often call after weeks of unopened post, and a frightened person cannot take in options until they feel heard. Brief the team to use one label early, such as: it sounds like the letters have been piling up and it has been hard to know where to start. Then stay silent for four seconds. Before bad news, use an accusation audit: you are probably worried this will make things worse. Track how many first calls reach a full income and expenditure, and record signs of vulnerability so clients get the right support. Keep Voss's bargaining system for suppliers, never clients.
connects: Voss's advice on ranges and framing the cost of not acting rests on anchoring and loss aversion, two effects Kahneman helped establish.
Voss's black swans, hidden facts that change a whole negotiation once they surface, echo Taleb's warning that the unknown piece of information matters most.
Letting the other person talk, seeing their point of view and admitting fault first are Carnegie's rules rediscovered on a hostage line eighty years later.
recap:
In the autumn of nineteen ninety-three, a bank robbery in Brooklyn turned into a siege, and on the phone was a fairly new FBI negotiator called Chris Voss. The robber lied about almost everything. Nobody died. And Voss learned that negotiation was not really a contest of offers. It was the work of discovering what the other person believed was happening.

He had arrived there by accident. A knee injury ended his hopes of joining a SWAT team, so he volunteered on a suicide crisis line, and learned that you cannot argue a desperate person out of despair. You can only show them you understand, and let them talk their own way back. That took him into hostage negotiation, and from two thousand and three to two thousand and seven he was the Bureau's lead international kidnapping negotiator.

At Harvard Law School he beat the professors who had written the field by asking, again and again, how am I supposed to do that? It was a refusal with no no in it, and it handed them his problem to solve. In Haiti, his team discovered that kidnappers demanding a fortune really wanted money for Saturday night. In Baghdad, he watched deadlines for the reporter Jill Carroll come and go, until she walked free after eighty-two days.

Out of all this came tactical empathy, which is not sympathy and not agreement, but understanding someone's world and saying it out loud. Mirror their last few words and wait. Label the feeling you can hear. Before bad news, list every accusation they might make against you, and make it first. Give people the safety of saying no. And listen for the moment they say that's right, rather than you're right, because that is when they stop defending.

He also has a bargaining system, built on anchoring and shrinking concessions, but he insists it comes last. Haggling before you understand the other side is trading numbers in the dark.

Read him as a very good witness rather than a scientist. His stories are his own memories and cannot always be checked. His famous claim that only seven per cent of communication is words is a myth. And his attack on the Harvard school fights an old caricature. His tools are built for the hardest case, a frightened or hostile person holding the cards.

The line to remember is the one he learned on the crisis line. People need to be heard before they can be moved.
